extracted.intended_audience: government officials, military commanders, governors, and executive staff (1861 U.S. federal government)
extracted.subtask_description: Collection of presidential proclamations, orders, and correspondence setting legal, military, and administrative standards for conduct of the Civil War (Aug–Nov 1861). Includes instructions on proclamations, troop allocation, militia terms, and enforcement measures.

rubrics_metrics.name: National Fast-Day Proclamation (Aug 12, 1861)
rubrics_metrics.description: The President appoints the last Thursday in September as a day of humiliation, prayer, and fasting for all the people of the nation, recommending observance by ministers, teachers of religion, and heads of families according to their creeds and modes of worship.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Purpose: to acknowledge God's government, confess national sins, pray for pardon and blessings on the nation's arms, and for restoration of peace and civil and religious liberty. Observance should be in humility and religious solemnity so that the united prayer of the nation may 'bring down plentiful blessings upon our country.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Proclamation forbidding intercourse with insurrectionary states (Aug 16, 1861)
rubrics_metrics.description: Declares inhabitants of specified Southern States to be 'in a state of insurrection' and that all commercial intercourse between them (except loyal parts) and other parts of the United States is unlawful; goods, vessels, and vehicles coming from or going to such states without presidential (Treasury) license shall be forfeited.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Enforcement: forfeiture of goods and conveyances; ships and vessels of citizens of those states found at sea or in U.S. ports after fifteen days will be forfeited. District attorneys, marshals, revenue, military and naval officers are enjoined to enforce the act; aggrieved parties may apply to Secretary of the Treasury for remission if special circumstances require.

rubrics_metrics.name: Authorization to suspend the writ of habeas corpus (Oct 14, 1861)
rubrics_metrics.description: Extends the military line for suppression of the insurrection as far as Bangor, Maine, and authorizes the suspension of the writ of habeas corpus in any place between that place and the city of Washington by officers acting under the military authority.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is an order delegating authority to military commanders to suspend habeas corpus within the designated military line for purposes of insurrection suppression; it sets geographic bounds to the suspension authorization.

rubrics_metrics.name: Requirement that military proclamations conform to Acts of Congress (Fremont correspondence, Sept 2–11, 1861)
rubrics_metrics.description: Proclamations by military commanders must not exceed or conflict with provisions enacted by Congress (specifically: modify Fremont's confiscation/liberation clause to conform to the Act of Congress of Aug 6, 1861).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Lincoln orders modification so the proclamation's clause 'be so modified, held, and construed as to conform to, and not to transcend, the provisions' of the congressional act. Rationale: permanent changes in property or slavery are legislative functions and should not be unilaterally declared by military proclamation; political consequences (e.g., alienating Union friends in border states) must be considered.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limit on taking life under extra-judicial proclamations (Fremont correspondence, Sept 2, 1861)
rubrics_metrics.description: Before executing a person under the terms of a military proclamation (e.g., ordering shooting), the commanding general must first obtain the President's approbation or consent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rationale: unilateral executions under broad proclamations risk reciprocal reprisals and political fallout; death sentences or comparable extreme measures should require presidential approval.

rubrics_metrics.name: Principle distinguishing military necessity from permanent legislative acts (Letter to O. H. Browning, Sept 22, 1861)
rubrics_metrics.description: Military officers may seize property or slaves when needed for immediate military purposes, but permanently depriving owners of property or fixing the permanent condition of slaves is a legislative function reserved for laws passed by Congress, not military proclamations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Policy and legal limit: temporary military seizure is within military law, but permanent confiscation or emancipation should be enacted by Congress; proclamations that purport to effect permanent changes in property or personal status are 'purely political' and exceed military authority.

rubrics_metrics.name: Conditional delivery of sensitive communications to field commanders (Oct 24, 1861 instruction to Curtis)
rubrics_metrics.description: A sealed inclosure to Major-General Fremont is to be delivered only if, upon reaching him, he is not then in personal command having fought and won a battle, actually in battle, or in immediate presence of the enemy expecting a battle.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Operational security and timing: messages/orders may be withheld to avoid disrupting or endangering ongoing combat operations; sequence of deliveries to commanders (Fremont first, then Hunter) is prescribed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Campaign planning principles for the western theater (Memorandum for a Plan of Campaign, Oct 1? 1861)
rubrics_metrics.description: Proposes simultaneous operations for the coast and Cumberland Gap movements; recommends defensive vigilance and preparation until forces are ready; advises concentration of forces at Lexington then Thomas's camp, and thence upon the Gap; use of railroads to secure lines of communication and to reinforce points; avoid long, exhausting pursuits of retreating enemy forces.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Specifics: watch but do not attack Price or Buckner until coordinated movements begin; Sherman to stand fast during the Gap operation; commanders should assess mountain passes to find defensible approaches; the coast and Gap movements should be simultaneous to create diversion and advantage for McClellan and Fremont. Emphasis on logistics (guard railroads, secure supplies) and avoiding overextension.

rubrics_metrics.name: Regional troop allocation by origin (Memorandum for a Plan of Campaign)
rubrics_metrics.description: Suggested appropriation of troops by state/region to specific commanders: forces from Wisconsin, Minnesota, Iowa, Illinois, Missouri, and Kansas to Fremont; Indiana and Michigan to Anderson at Louisville; Ohio troops needed in western Virginia to be sent there with remainder to Mitchell at Cincinnati for Anderson; forces east of the mountains appropriated to McClellan and to the coast.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is a planning guideline for assigning recruitment/available state contingents to departmental commanders to streamline reinforcement and operational command.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of corps-of-observation and railroad termini for Missouri defense (Memo re Department of the West advice)
rubrics_metrics.description: After pursuing Price, give up long pursuit and halt main army; divide into two corps of observation occupying Sedalia and Rolla (railroad termini), reestablish discipline, improve equipment and quarters, and guard and keep open both railroads with judicious force.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rationale: holding and protecting railheads creates defensible bases, allows concentration to repel return invasions, and permits surplus forces to be reallocated as needed. Avoid attempting to reach distant objectives via long circuitous routes that exhaust forces.

rubrics_metrics.name: Terms and conditions for State militia service paid by United States (Order approving Governor Gamble's Plan, Nov 5, 1861)
rubrics_metrics.description: Missouri proposes to raise a State militia to serve within the State as State militia during the war, to cooperate with U.S. troops; the militia is to be embodied, drilled, disciplined, and governed according to Army Regulations and subject to the Articles of War; not to be ordered out of the State except for immediate defense; to be armed, equipped, clothed, subsisted, transported, and paid by the United States while actually embodied and in service.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Command relationship: when State militia officers act with U.S. officers of the same grade, U.S. officers shall command the combined force. Financial/staff limits: to avoid burdening the Treasury, the U.S. will pay only specified staff (adjutant-general, quartermaster-general, inspector-general) though State law may authorize more; the number of aides-de-camp reported for U.S. payment limited to three. Disbursing officers shall be assigned by the War Department where necessary; President may require regulations to insure regularity of returns and to protect the U.S. from fraud.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limits on staff ranks and pay for state militia serving with U.S. (Order approving Governor Gamble's Plan)
rubrics_metrics.description: Although State law may create numerous staff officers (each with the rank of colonel), the Governor proposes that the U.S. Government pay only the adjutant-general, quartermaster-general, and inspector-general (and that only three aides-de-camp be reported for payment). Field officers and company officer structure specified (one colonel, one lieutenant-colonel, one major per regiment; captain, first lieutenant, second lieutenant per company).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Purpose: to limit federal expenditure on redundant state staff while accommodating state organizational law; compensation from U.S. limited to ranks and pay corresponding to act of Congress of July 22, 1861 for officers performing equivalent duties in U.S. service.

rubrics_metrics.name: Administrative procedures upon change of army command (General Orders No. 94 / Nov 1, 1861)
rubrics_metrics.description: Upon placing Brevet Lieutenant-General Winfield Scott on retired list and appointing Major-General George B. McClellan to assume command, the headquarters of the army will be established in Washington; all communications intended for the commanding general to be addressed direct to the adjutant-general; duplicate returns, orders, and other papers previously sent to the assistant adjutant-general, headquarters of the army, will be discontinued.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Establishes protocol for communications and paper flow when a new commanding general assumes command to centralize correspondence and discontinue obsolete duplicate reporting channels.

rubrics_metrics.name: Secrecy and discretion in commissioning (Sept 17 letter re Simon B. Buckner)
rubrics_metrics.description: Make out a commission for Simon B. Buckner as brigadier-general of volunteers and put it into the hands of General Anderson to deliver to Buckner or not, at Anderson's discretion; the commission is to remain secret unless and until delivered.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use of secrecy and local discretion for appointments: commissions may be prepared and withheld to be delivered at the appropriate time and place as determined by field commanders to avoid political or operational complications.
